newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea puts Hanbo Steel up for auction.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea puts Hanbo Steel up for auction.

text.p: South Korea has announced plans to auction off the troubled Hanbo Steel Co, but the the Hyundai Group, seen by analysts as a possible buyer, said on Thursday it was not interested.
An official at Korea First Bank, the stricken steelmaker's prime creditor bank, said Hanbo would be sold in a public auction.
"We plan to sell Hanbo Steel through a public auction because that appears to be the best way," he said, adding that details on the sale date and minimum bid have not been set yet.
If the first auction fails, creditor banks would hold additional auctions, he said.
"If that doesn't work out, we'll seek a third-party takeover of Hanbo Steel through private negotiations with interested parties," the official said.
Hanbo Steel, flagship of Hanbo Group, collapsed in January after piling up five trillion won ($5.6 billion) in debt.

Analysts said Hyundai, the country's biggest conglomerate in terms of assets, was the obvious potential buyer because it has been trying to enter the steel-making business and had the financial standing to take over Hanbo Steel.
But a Hyundai Group spokesman brushed aside the speculation.
"We have no plan to take over Hanbo," the spokesman said. "We are only interested in starting an integrated steel mill using blast furnaces. We don't want Hanbo's electric-arc furnace."
Hyundai has made no secret of its interest in building an integrated steel mill.

The government, although it has not directly opposed Hyundai in public, has voiced concerns about an oversupply of steel and approving anything that would increase the concentration of economic power in the country's big conglomerates.
Analysts said Hyundai was probably more interested than it was letting on.
"Hyundai is denying its interest in order to secure a better bargaining position in take-over negotiations," said Sohn Soo-yeon, a steel analyst at ING-Barings Securities.
Analysts said Hyundai was likely to later propose to take over Hanbo in return for government approval to build an integrated steel mill.
Hyundai Group is the country's biggest consumer of steel.
"Hyundai wants integrated steelmaking to secure a stable supply of steel products for its production of cars, ships and home appliances," said Sohn of ING-Barings.

When completed, Hanbo's steel mill, located in the southern city of Tangjin, would have an annual capacity of seven million tonnes. That would place Hanbo among the world's top 15 steel producers and would make it South Korea's second largest after Pohang Iron and Steel (POSCO), analysts said.
But analysts said Hyundai would gain minimal benefits from acquiring Hanbo Steel.

"There is no merit. The quality of steel products produced from Hanbo's electric furnace is inferior to those from Pohang Iron and Steel's blast furnace," said Park Jun-hyung, a steel analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.
Park said it would be difficult for Hyundai to use steel produced by Hanbo for its high-quality consumer durables.

Analysts said Hanbo's electric-arc furnace would be cheaper and would generate less pollution than POSCO's integrated steel mill. But Hanbo's product would be of lower quality than that turned out by POSCO's more sophisticated mill, they said.

Analysts also said a court-appointed management team's forecast for Hanbo Steel to post a profit from the year 2001 was too optimistic. "Hanbo could probably post a profit 10 years from now," said Park of Jardine Fleming.
